accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE KS3 physics programme of study (non-contact forces: weight = mass × gravitational field strength g; on Earth g = 10 N/kg, different on other planets) and NGSS MS-PS2-4. Field strengths used: Earth 10 (rounded from 9.8), Moon 1.6, Mars 3.7, Jupiter 25 N/kg, matching NASA planetary fact sheet surface gravities to two figures (1.62, 3.71, 24.8). Every lab number recomputed: 5×10=50, 60×1.6=96, 2×25=50; 37÷3.7=10, 80÷1.6=50, 250÷25=10; the bag reads 20, 3.2, 7.4 and 50 N. Parameterised answers m*10, m, m*25 and 10*k are whole numbers at both corners of each range.

misconceptions.evidence: Wrong options are built from the slips listed in the adult notes and named in feedback: kg used as a weight unit (the 2 kg newtonmeter option), mass shrinking on the Moon (the 0.3 kg prediction), no gravity on the Moon (0 kg), adding m and g (15 N, 61.6 N, 27 N distractors), and multiplying by g on the way back (8,000 kg, 136.9 kg, 6250 kg). The wrong-path script clicked each one and every message states the specific error, e.g. '3 N forgets g. Multiply by 10 N/kg'.

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed under the 30% shingle limit. No other lab pairs a spring newtonmeter with a weight-against-mass graph and an equal-arm balance that stays level while the meter changes across four worlds; lesson 569 uses non-standard units for ages 5 to 6 and has no field strength. The two-way W = m × g and m = W ÷ g rounds and the eight-card mass/weight sort are specific to this topic.

lab_teaches.evidence: Six steps build the idea in order: hang 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 kg and see the points make a straight line through 0 with slope 10 N per kg; take the same 2 kg bag to the Moon, Mars and Jupiter where the meter changes but the balance still levels at 2 kg; calculate weights; divide back to masses; sort statements; then the challenge. Each step ends with a stated rule rather than a bare tick.

predictions.evidence: Three locked-in predictions before the reveal: the 2 kg meter reading on Earth (20 N vs 2 N vs 2 kg), what happens to mass on the Moon (stays 2 kg, drops to 0.3 kg, becomes 0 kg) and the mass of an 800 N astronaut (80 vs 800 vs 8,000 kg). The feedback repeats the learner's own choice and says whether it was spot on, as seen in the 360 px light and dark screenshots.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge step cycles through a bank of questions on Earth, Mars, Jupiter and the Moon, both W = m × g and m = W ÷ g, with the answer order rotated. The wrong-path run picked 3 N for a 3 kg bag on Earth and got '✗ 3 N forgets g. Multiply by 10 N/kg: 3 × 10 = 30 N. Another →'; the add, divide and times-again slips each have their own message. Correct picks give a tick and a streak count, and Restart resets every step.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation FK grade 1.8 overall (paragraphs 2.4, 3.3, 3.1, -0.6), well under the 6.5 limit for 11 to 12 year olds, with the terms mass, weight, newton and g each introduced once with a meaning. Adult notes FK 7.0, under 9.5. Lab captions and step titles are short; the long sort-step done banner was cut to 'Mass: kg, same everywhere. Weight: N, a force.' after it ran to three lines.

no_filler.evidence: gate_content passed with explanation overlap under 12%. Every kid paragraph carries a fact the later items test (balance vs newtonmeter, g = 10 N/kg on Earth, 3.2 N on the Moon, 50 N on Jupiter); the adult notes give the curriculum statements, the instrument contrast including bathroom scales, and the named mistakes; there are no motivational lines.

mobile.evidence: Screenshot QA at 360 × 640 in both themes showed the world buttons overlapping the newtonmeter scale in Other worlds; the meter now starts below the button row (MTOP offset) and the buttons read Earth/Moon/Mars/Jupiter in full. Every canvas action also has a full-size HTML button (Hang 0.5 kg, Balance with 2 kg, the answer choices), so nothing needs precise dragging on a phone.

accessibility.evidence: gate_browser passed: axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13, Show me finished each step with a tick, and there were no console or page errors in either screenshot run. The canvas sits on a light card in dark mode, keeps a live aria-label updated with each reading (e.g. 'Jupiter: the newtonmeter reads 50 N, but the balance still levels with 2 kg'), and the buttons mirror every canvas action for keyboard users.
